subject: surgery
title: Invasive Lobular Carcinoma, E-Cadherin Loss, and Bilateral Disease

steps.tx: Representing ten to fifteen percent of all invasive breast malignancies, **invasive lobular carcinoma** is the second most common histological subtype following invasive ductal carcinoma. It arises from the terminal duct lobular unit and exhibits a unique biology characterized by discohesive, single-cell infiltration. Because lobular carcinoma expands through subtle permeation without provoking an intense desmoplastic connective tissue reaction, it frequently presents as an indistinct thickening rather than a hard lump.
steps.say: Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common breast cancer, characterized by discohesive single cells infiltrating without forming a dense mass, often presenting as diffuse thickening.

vis.alt: Histological and clinical diagram comparing invasive lobular carcinoma with invasive ductal carcinoma.
vis.caption: Invasive breast cancer subtypes: lobular carcinoma single-cell streaming versus ductal carcinoma cohesive tubules. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The genetic and molecular hallmark defining invasive lobular carcinoma is the complete **loss of E-cadherin expression**. Encoded by the CDH1 gene on chromosome 16q22, E-cadherin is a transmembrane calcium-dependent cell adhesion molecule that anchors adjacent epithelial cells together via cytoplasmic catenin complexes. Inactivating mutations, deletions, or promoter hypermethylation of CDH1 disrupt E-cadherin synthesis, stripping cells of intercellular adhesion and driving a dyscohesive, single-file migratory phenotype.
steps.say: Loss of E-cadherin due to CDH1 gene mutations is the hallmark of lobular cancer. Without this adhesion molecule, tumor cells lose contact inhibition and infiltrate in single file.

steps.tx: On microscopic examination, this discohesive growth manifests as the classic histopathological pattern known as **Indian filing of tumor cells**. Small, uniform, rounded neoplastic cells march in long, slender, single-file cords through collagenous stroma without distorting underlying ductal architecture. Furthermore, lobular cells characteristically encircle normal, uninvolved mammary ducts in concentric laminated rings, an architectural hallmark termed targetoid infiltration.
steps.say: Microscopy reveals Indian filing, where small uniform tumor cells stream in single file through connective tissue, often encircling normal ducts in a targetoid pattern.

steps.tx: The tumour cells here march through stroma in single files rather than forming cohesive glands, encircling ducts in a targetoid fashion. This **Indian filing** reflects lost E-cadherin adhesion, confirmed when immunostaining comes back negative. Recognising the pattern explains why lobular cancers hide on imaging, grow multifocally, and so often involve the opposite breast as well.
steps.say: Single-file Indian filing with negative E-cadherin defines lobular carcinoma. Lost adhesion explains its diffuse, often bilateral growth.

vis.caption: Invasive lobular carcinoma histology showing single-file Indian filing cells with absent E-cadherin staining. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: To definitively distinguish challenging poorly differentiated ductal carcinomas from pleomorphic lobular carcinomas, pathologists perform immunohistochemical staining for E-cadherin. Invasive ductal carcinoma displays intense, continuous membranous brown staining, whereas invasive lobular carcinoma demonstrates **negative E-cadherin immunostaining**. Occasionally, lobular carcinoma cells contain intracytoplasmic mucin droplets that compress the nucleus against the cell membrane, forming classic signet ring cells.
steps.say: Immunohistochemistry confirms lobular cancer by demonstrating complete absence of E-cadherin staining, distinguishing it from ductal carcinoma which stains strongly positive.

steps.tx: A defining clinical feature of invasive lobular carcinoma is its propensity for **multifocality, multicentricity, and bilaterality**. Bilateral synchronous or metachronous breast cancer develops in ten to twenty percent of patients with lobular carcinoma, a rate nearly double that observed in ductal carcinoma. Furthermore, because cells permeate without inciting desmoplasia, conventional mammography frequently fails to delineate the true tumor extent, underestimating lesion volume in up to forty percent.
steps.say: Lobular carcinoma is bilateral in up to twenty percent of patients and frequently multifocal. Because it elicits little desmoplasia, mammography often severely underestimates tumor volume.

steps.tx: To overcome the limitations of mammography in staging lobular carcinoma, high-field **preoperative dynamic contrast MRI** of both breasts is strongly recommended. Dynamic breast MRI boasts a sensitivity exceeding ninety-five percent for invasive lobular carcinoma, accurately mapping the full three-dimensional extent of disease, detecting occult multicentric ipsilateral satellite foci, and uncovering unsuspected synchronous contralateral breast malignancies prior to definitive surgical resection.
steps.say: Preoperative dynamic contrast breast MRI is recommended for lobular carcinoma. It accurately measures tumor extent and identifies hidden multicentric or contralateral tumors.

steps.tx: Invasive lobular carcinoma exhibits an atypical, distinct pattern of distant metastatic dissemination compared to ductal cancer. While ductal cancer metastasizes predominantly to the lungs, liver, brain, and skeleton, lobular carcinoma displays an affinity for **peritoneal and gastrointestinal metastasis**. It infiltrates the peritoneum, retroperitoneum, omentum, stomach, colon, and ovaries, producing a clinical picture mimicking linitis plastica, bilateral Krukenberg tumors, or malignant bowel obstruction.
steps.say: Lobular carcinoma spreads to unique metastatic sites, infiltrating the peritoneum, retroperitoneum, stomach, and ovaries, mimicking linitis plastica and gastrointestinal obstruction.

steps.tx: Surgical management of invasive lobular carcinoma is complicated by significantly higher rates of positive surgical margins during breast-conserving surgery, requiring re-excision or conversion to mastectomy in up to twenty-five percent of cases. Because virtually all lobular carcinomas are strongly estrogen-receptor positive and HER2-negative, **adjuvant endocrine therapy with aromatase inhibitors** (such as letrozole or anastrozole) is exceptionally effective, serving as the therapeutic backbone of systemic adjuvant management.
steps.say: Lobular cancer has a higher rate of positive margins during breast-conserving surgery. Because over ninety-five percent are hormone-positive, aromatase inhibitors are highly effective.
